steps.title: What health actually is
steps.body:
The **World Health Organization** (WHO) defines health as *a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity*.

That definition is wider than most people expect. Someone with no disease at all can still be unhealthy: lonely, anxious, or without enough food. And someone with a well-managed condition, such as asthma, can be healthy.

A **disease** is a condition that stops part of the body working properly. The rest of this unit is about what causes diseases, how they spread, how the body fights them, and how medicines are made to help.

steps.title: Communicable and non-communicable
steps.body:
**Communicable** diseases are caused by **pathogens** and can be passed from one person, animal or plant to another: cholera, tuberculosis, malaria.

**Non-communicable** diseases cannot be passed on: coronary heart disease, most cancers, type 2 diabetes. They usually come from a mix of factors, such as genes and lifestyle, and they are the subject of the last topic in this unit.

The two are linked. **Having one disease can make you more likely to get another.** HIV destroys white blood cells, so the immune system is weakened and infections such as tuberculosis take hold. Being malnourished weakens the body in the same way. This is why a disease in one part of a population can drive others up with it.

steps.title: Four kinds of pathogen
steps.body:
A **pathogen** is a microorganism that causes disease. There are four kinds on the specification, and each named disease belongs to one of them — learn them as pairs.

- **Bacteria**: single cells with no nucleus. Many release toxins. *Cholera, tuberculosis, stomach ulcers (Helicobacter), Chlamydia.*
- **Viruses**: not cells at all — genetic material in a protein coat. They can only reproduce inside a host cell. *HIV, Ebola.*
- **Fungi**: some are single cells, others grow threads through tissue; many spread by spores. *Chalara ash dieback.*
- **Protists**: single cells with a nucleus. *Malaria.*

The kind of pathogen matters later: **antibiotics only work on bacteria**, which is why they are useless against HIV.

steps.title: The named diseases and what they do
steps.body:
The specification names seven infections. For each, know three things: the **pathogen**, what it **does**, and — in the next step — how it **spreads**.

Two of them, stomach ulcers caused by *Helicobacter* and Ebola, are Biology-only content; since you are sitting separate Biology, they are yours to learn.

The table is worth learning by heart. Exam questions often give one column and ask for another.

steps.title: How they spread, and how to stop them
steps.body:
Every control measure works the same way: **find the route the pathogen uses, and cut it**. That is the sentence to carry into every question on this.

- **Water** (cholera): clean drinking water and treated sewage.
- **Airborne** (tuberculosis, Chalara): for TB, ventilation, covering coughs, isolating patients and the BCG vaccine; for Chalara, removing and burning infected trees and limiting the movement of ash plants.
- **Animal vectors** (malaria): a **vector** carries a pathogen between hosts. Stop the mosquito with nets, insecticide and draining standing water.
- **Oral transmission** (stomach ulcers): hygiene, and safe food and water.
- **Body fluids** (Ebola): isolating patients, protective clothing, safe burial.

steps.title: Spotting and identifying plant disease
steps.body:
Before a plant disease can be controlled, it has to be **detected** and the cause **identified**. That is done in two places.

**In the field**
- **Observe the symptoms**: spots or patches on leaves, discoloured or wilting leaves, stunted growth, rotting, unusual growths, or visible pests.
- **Look at the distribution**: map which plants are affected. A pathogen tends to spread outwards from where it started, while a pattern that follows the land — the wettest corner, one soil type — points to a cause in the environment.
- **Eliminate environmental causes**: frost, waterlogging and a shortage of minerals in the soil can all produce similar symptoms, so rule them out.

**In the lab**
- **Diagnostic testing** identifies the pathogen itself: examining samples under a microscope, growing the microorganism, or using a DNA test or a kit containing antibodies that bind only to that pathogen.

steps.title: Viruses: the lytic and lysogenic pathways
steps.body:
A virus cannot reproduce on its own; it has to use a host cell. There are two ways it can go.

**The lytic pathway.** The virus **attaches** to a cell and **injects** its genetic material. The cell is taken over: it **copies** the viral genetic material and makes viral proteins, which **assemble** into new viruses. Then the cell **bursts** — *lysis* — releasing them to infect more cells.

**The lysogenic pathway.** The viral genetic material is **inserted into the host's DNA**. Every time the cell divides, the viral genes are copied too, so they spread through new cells without doing any damage. They lie **dormant** until a trigger switches them into the lytic pathway.

This is why some viral infections cause symptoms long after the person was infected.

steps.title: Sexually transmitted infections
steps.body:
**Sexually transmitted infections** (STIs) are spread by sexual contact. The specification names two, and they are different kinds of pathogen, which matters for treatment.

**Chlamydia** is a **bacterium**. It often causes no symptoms, so people pass it on without knowing, and it can lead to infertility. Because it is a bacterium, it can be cured with **antibiotics**.

**HIV** is a **virus**. As well as sex, it spreads through **blood** — shared needles, and from mother to baby. Antibiotics do not work on it, but **antiretroviral drugs** reduce the amount of virus.

Reducing spread: **condoms** for both; **screening** so infected people are found and treated; and for HIV, not sharing needles and screening donated blood.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Chlamydia and HIV: pathogen, how each spreads, treatment and how spread is reduced

check.prompt: Which measure reduces the spread of both Chlamydia and HIV?
check.solution: **Condoms** stop the transfer of body fluids during sex, which is how both spread. Antibiotics treat only Chlamydia.

steps.title: Your turn: disease, pathogen, route, control
steps.body:
Cover the table from the last two steps and try to rebuild it: for each named disease, the pathogen, the route, and one way to cut the route. Then check.

The pattern to notice: **the control always matches the route**. If you know how a disease spreads, you can work out a sensible control even for a disease you have never met, which is exactly what the harder questions ask.

steps.title: Going deeper: routes, chains and unfamiliar diseases
steps.body:
Three habits mark out the top answers in this topic.

**Tie every control to the route.** *Use nets* earns less than *use nets, so mosquitoes cannot bite and pass on the protist*. The examiner wants to see that you know **why** the measure works.

**Write chains, not lists, for *explain* questions.** Why does HIV make TB more likely? Destroys white blood cells → immune system weakened → TB bacteria not destroyed. Each link follows from the last.

**Transfer to the unfamiliar.** The harder questions give a disease you have not met — spread by ticks, by fleas, by shared cups. Classify the route, then reach for the control you would use for the named disease with the same route.

And for the Biology-only virus lifecycle: know the **order** of the lytic pathway, and that the lysogenic pathway explains **delayed** symptoms.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Health** (WHO): complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
- **Communicable** diseases are caused by pathogens and spread; **non-communicable** ones do not.
- **One disease can raise the risk of another**: HIV destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system, so TB takes hold.
- **Four pathogens**: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists. Learn each named disease with its pathogen.
- **Named infections**: cholera (bacterium, diarrhoea), tuberculosis (bacterium, lung damage), Chalara (fungus, leaf loss and bark lesions), malaria (protist, blood and liver), HIV (virus, white blood cells, AIDS), stomach ulcers (*Helicobacter*), Ebola (virus, haemorrhagic fever).
- **Routes**: water, airborne, animal vectors, oral transmission, body fluids. **The control always cuts the route.**
- **Viruses**: lytic — attach, inject, copy, assemble, burst; lysogenic — inserted into host DNA, dormant, later lytic.
- **Plant disease** is detected in the field (symptoms, distribution, ruling out environmental causes) and identified in the lab by diagnostic testing.
- **STIs**: Chlamydia (bacterium, antibiotics) and HIV (virus, antiretrovirals); condoms and screening for both.

questions.prompt: Explain how the spread of malaria can be reduced.
questions.solution: Two chains, because malaria has a vector and a pathogen. Stop the mosquito: nets treated with insecticide, spraying insecticide, draining standing water where mosquitoes breed — so fewer bites and fewer mosquitoes carry the protist. Treat people: antimalarial drugs kill the protist, so infected people cannot pass it on when bitten.

questions.modelAnswer: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, so one way is to stop people being bitten: sleeping under nets treated with insecticide means infected mosquitoes cannot reach them, so fewer people are infected. Draining standing water removes the places where mosquitoes lay their eggs, so there are fewer mosquitoes to carry the protist. Treating infected people with antimalarial drugs kills the protist in their blood, so a mosquito that bites them cannot pick it up and pass it on.

questions.prompt: Why can a virus following the lysogenic pathway cause symptoms years after infection?
questions.solution: In the lysogenic pathway the viral genetic material sits **dormant** inside the host's DNA, copied along with it, causing no symptoms. A trigger later switches it into the **lytic** pathway, when new viruses are made and cells burst.

questions.prompt: Compare how cholera and Ebola are spread, and how the spread of each can be reduced.
questions.solution: Organise by feature, both diseases in each point. Pathogen: both are microorganisms but cholera is a bacterium, Ebola a virus. Spread: cholera through contaminated water, Ebola through body fluids. Reduction: cholera by clean water and sewage treatment, which protects whole communities; Ebola by isolating patients, protective clothing for carers and safe burial, which targets contact with individuals.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): facts about one disease, or both described separately
Level 2 (3 to 4): some comparison of spread or control
Level 3 (5 to 6): spread and control compared for both, with how each measure works

criteria.text: Spread compared: contaminated water against body fluids
Control compared: clean water and sanitation against isolation and protective equipment
Why each control works, tied to how that disease spreads

questions.modelAnswer: Both are communicable diseases, but they spread in very different ways. Cholera bacteria are carried in **water** contaminated with infected faeces, whereas the Ebola virus passes directly through the **body fluids** of infected people, such as blood or vomit. Because of that, the controls differ. Cholera is reduced by providing **clean drinking water** and **treating sewage**, which breaks the route for a whole community at once. Ebola is reduced by **isolating** patients, giving carers **protective clothing**, and burying the dead safely, all of which stop contact with body fluids. In each case the control works by cutting the particular route the pathogen uses.

questions.prompt: HIV is described as leading to AIDS. What is AIDS?
questions.solution: HIV destroys white blood cells. **AIDS** is the stage when so many are destroyed that the immune system can no longer fight off other infections, such as tuberculosis, which then take hold.

questions.prompt: A fungal tree disease starts to spread across a country. Which action would do most to slow it?
questions.solution: Like Chalara, a fungal disease spreads by airborne spores. Removing and burning infected trees destroys the source of spores, and restricting movement stops infected saplings carrying it to new areas. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, trees cannot be vaccinated, and draining water is a malaria measure.

examTechnique.body:
Topic 5 is on Paper 1, and this part of it is a knowledge test before it is anything else: each named disease with its pathogen, its effect and its route. Learn the table until any one column gives you the other two, because questions routinely give one and ask for another.

The marks above the recall are for reasoning. A control measure scores when it is tied to the route it cuts. An *explain* answer scores when it is a chain in which each step follows from the last. And the hardest questions give a disease you have never met, where the method is to classify its route and apply the control you would use for a named disease with the same route.
examinerErrors: Calling a virus a bacterium, or suggesting antibiotics for HIV or Ebola. Antibiotics only work on bacteria.
Naming a control without saying why it works: *use nets* rather than *nets stop mosquitoes biting and passing on the protist*.
Mixing up the routes: cholera is water-borne, tuberculosis airborne, Ebola through body fluids.
Describing malaria as a bacterial or viral disease. It is caused by a protist, carried by a mosquito vector.
Explaining why HIV makes TB likely without the middle link: that the immune system is weakened because white blood cells are destroyed.
Confusing the lytic and lysogenic pathways. Lytic ends with the cell bursting; lysogenic inserts viral genes into the host DNA, where they lie dormant.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer knows every named disease across all three columns — pathogen, effect, route — without hesitation. It ties each control measure to the route it breaks, writes explanations as chains in which each link causes the next, and handles an unfamiliar disease by classifying its route and reasoning from the named disease that shares it. On viruses it gives the lytic pathway in order and uses the lysogenic pathway to explain symptoms that appear long after infection.
